objectives: Slide a window of fixed size across an array or string in O(n).
Update a window's summary with one value entering and one leaving.
Keep counts for the letters inside a window.

sections.heading: Intuition: slide, don't recompute
paragraphs: A window is a run of consecutive values. When a fixed-size window moves one step right, only two values change: one enters on the right and one leaves on the left. Everything else in the window stays the same.
So don't recompute the window's sum or counts from scratch. Keep them as running state and update them with the two values that changed. That turns O(n·k) into O(n).

callout.text: For each step, write down what the value entering does to your state and what the value leaving does. Do both, in an order that keeps the window exactly k wide.

diagram.description: Values 6, 1, 5, 2 with a window of two. Moving right, 6 leaves and 5 enters.

sections.heading: Baseline: add up every window from scratch
paragraphs: For each of the n - k + 1 windows, add its k values. That's O(n·k). With n = 100,000 and k = 50,000, it's billions of additions.

sections.heading: Worked example: windows with no repeated letter
paragraphs: Count the windows of k letters where no letter appears twice. Keep a count per letter in the window, and one more number: repeats, how many letters currently appear at least twice.

When a letter enters and its count becomes 2, repeats goes up. When a letter leaves and its count drops back to 1, repeats goes down. A window is good when repeats is 0. Tracking repeats means you never scan the counts to check a window.

sections.heading: Complexity and cautions
paragraphs: A fixed-size sliding window is O(n) time. Its memory is O(1) for a sum, or O(alphabet size) for letter counts.
Handle the first window separately or guard the "leaving" update so it only runs once the window is full. When k is larger than the input, there are no windows at all.

sections.heading: Before you finish
paragraphs: Try to answer each question before opening it.

checks.prompt: A window over [6, 1, 5, 2] moves from [6, 1] to [1, 5]. What changes in its sum?
checks.answer: Add 5 and subtract 6: the sum goes from 7 to 6.

checks.prompt: Why keep a repeats counter instead of scanning all counts for each window?
checks.answer: Scanning costs the alphabet size per window. The counter changes only when a count crosses 2, which you see as it happens.

checks.prompt: How many windows of size k does an array of length n have?
checks.answer: n - k + 1, or none if k > n.
